claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy has high configurational disorder in its as-prepared state.
The superconducting state of the selected alloy is uncharacterized.
Systematic thermal annealing can incrementally increase short-range chemical order in the alloy.
Annealing can enhance local ordering without causing phase separation.
Short-range chemical order locally modifies the bonding environment.
Short-range chemical order can be monitored using X-ray diffraction or pair-distribution-function measurements.
Increasing short-range chemical order reduces electron scattering caused by compositional randomness.
Reducing compositional-randomness scattering enhances electron–phonon interactions.
Electron–phonon interactions support Cooper-pair formation in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling will increase the superconducting transition temperature.
Enhanced local chemical order will elevate the superconducting transition temperature of the alloy.
Enhanced local chemical order will modify the alloy's critical magnetic fields.
A subset of high-entropy alloys becomes type-II superconducting at cryogenic temperatures.
Annealed samples will have a statistically significantly higher transition temperature than pristine samples.
The as-prepared alloy has a lower transition temperature, if superconductivity is detectable.
The proposed ordering effect is limited to annealing conditions that avoid secondary phases and long-range crystallographic changes.
Impurity formation may obscure the relationship between short-range order and superconductivity.
A lack of statistically significant transition-temperature enhancement or of correlation between ordering and superconducting enhancement would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Critical-field changes are described as only potential in the prediction, but the falsification rule uses absence of critical-field modification as an independent reason to falsify the hypothesis, even if Tc increases.
